title: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma
tomorrow: desire and will on a sacred list? what are they doing there?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four mahavakyas read two ways: Shankara's one without a second, Ramanuja's Brahman dwelling within the knower. Today the Aitareya looks out the window.

Early morning, before the phone comes on. A bird on the fence. A weed pushing up through a crack in the driveway. The neighbor's dog, stretching. The Aitareya Upanishad has its own version of that window, and it's crowded: sprouts and birds, horses, cows, elephants, wind and water and fire, the open sky, and the gods by name. One thing, the text says, is true of every one of them.
screen: `A BIRD. A WEED. A DOG.` → `THE AITAREYA'S CROWDED WINDOW.` → `ONE THING TRUE OF ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Having pointed at the knowing inside a person, the Aitareya turns outward. This is Brahman, it says. This is Indra, this is Prajapati, these are all the gods. These are the great elements: earth, wind, space, water, light. The creatures born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, from sprouts. Horses, cows, people, elephants. Whatever breathes, whatever moves, whatever flies, and whatever stands still. All of it is guided by prajnana, and rests in prajnana. Then a short phrase worth keeping: prajnanetro lokah. The world has knowing for its eye. Two things stand out. First, the gods are on the list. Indra and Prajapati aren't above the knowing, steering it. They're among the things it guides. Second, it reaches past people. The elephant and the sprout are held by the same knowing the text found, a few lines earlier, inside a person. And notice what the Upanishad doesn't say. It doesn't say a weed thinks, or that a sparrow does philosophy. It says each one is guided by the knowing and rests in it, the way a whole scene rests in the eye that sees it. So prajnanam brahma isn't only a private light behind one pair of eyes. In this passage it's also the eye the whole world is seen by.
screen: `GODS, ELEMENTS, EVERY CREATURE.` · `THE WORLD HAS KNOWING FOR ITS EYE.` · `THE GODS ARE ON THE LIST.` · `HELD BY IT, NOT THINKING LIKE US.` · then, large: `PRAJNANETRO LOKAH.`

segments.voice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are: a plant, a tree through the window, a bird, even your own hand. Look at it for the whole sit without naming it. Let it simply be seen, and rest in the seeing, with the text's phrase in the background: the world has knowing for its eye.
The four mahavakyas, and prajnanam brahma at its widest: gods, elements, elephants and sprouts, all guided by the knowing.
Carry this: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma, where the whole world has knowing for its eye. That's day 1740.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Aitareya study this outward list together with the list of inner powers before it, so the saying prajnanam brahma is heard as covering both the inner life and the whole world.

original.note: Sanskrit prajnanetro lokah: the world (loka) has knowing (prajnana) for its eye (netra). From the lines just before prajnanam brahma.

prajnana.meaning: knowing; that by which anything is seen or heard

prajnanetro lokah.meaning: the world has knowing for its eye

mahavakyas.meaning: the great sayings, gathered by tradition from the Upanishads
